rationale: B wins because it keeps its hands cleaner: it turns the same four lanes into reporter-shaped stories without decorating the facts to make them sexier. A's "Airbnb's New Business-Ready Badge Asks Hosts to Upgrade. Many Won't Qualify." is a good story shape with a bad unproved conclusion stapled to the headline. B's "Airbnb says business trips grew 71% — the real story is the base it isn't sizing" is the sharper editorial move because it gates the pitch on proof instead of pretending the caveat is already a story.
gaps_in_A: "Many Won't Qualify" is an invented conclusion. The update gives badge requirements, not host qualification rates.
"Targeting the Market Navan Built" overreaches. Navan, TravelPerk, Booking.com for Business, and hotel corporate programs may be plausible context, but they are not in the supplied facts.
"the compliance gap that blocked corporate adoption" is an asserted market diagnosis, not a fact from the update.
"Ramp has been a fast-growing player" adds outside color the prompt did not provide. Small line, same bad habit: making the room look fuller than it is.
gaps_in_B: "journalist-fit-check" is the wrong next operational step if no journalist list exists yet. Pick the angle and build the list first, then fit-check names one by one.
"expense platforms are turning into the system of record" is a little grand for one Airbnb integration announcement. It is framed as a testable thesis, but it still needs restraint.
The host angle asks for qualification cost and booking lift, but misses the most obvious supply proof: how many US and UK listings actually qualify on day one.
The first angle could name the competitive set as proof to pursue, but wisely should not imply more competitive displacement than the facts support. It stays mostly clean, just a bit under-specified.
